title: Chayei Sarah: the life of Sarah
hookLine: a portion called "the life of Sarah" begins with her death

lines: CHAYEI SARAH: THE LIFE OF SARAH.
cards: Sarah dies in the first two verses of a Torah portion named for her life. It's called Chayei Sarah, the life of Sarah. It tells how long she lived, then that she died, then that Abraham came to mourn her.
Every year, Jews read a portion named for her life that opens with her death. Readers have made something of that. Today: why the name is life.

teach.b: Portions take their names from words near their start, and here the first words are these, in the Jewish Publication Society's old translation: "And the life of Sarah was a hundred and seven and twenty years; these were the years of the life of Sarah."
It doesn't say Sarah died at a hundred and twenty-seven. It says her life was that long, and then it says so again.

teach.h: A HUNDRED, TWENTY AND SEVEN YEARS.
teach.b: The Hebrew counts strangely, too: a hundred years, and twenty years, and seven years, each with its own word for years. Rashi, the medieval commentator, read that slowly.
Each stage is counted on its own, he said, because each was whole. At a hundred she was as free of wrongdoing as she had been at twenty, and at twenty as lovely as at seven.
And the closing phrase, these were the years of the life of Sarah: Rashi says all of them were equally good. Not only the well-known ones. The waiting years, the laughing year, the old years.
There's a harder side, too. The portion comes right after Abraham takes Isaac up the mountain, and an old midrash connects the two: Sarah died, it says, when she heard what had happened to her son.
The text itself is silent about that.

teach.h: ABRAHAM CAME TO MOURN AND WEEP.
teach.b: What it does say is that Abraham came to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her.

So the portion holds both: a real death, real grief, and a name that points past it. Readers take the name as a lesson: when you remember someone, you choose which word goes on the door. Here, the word is life.

how: Chayei Sarah is read in synagogues each autumn, and many Jews remember loved ones by telling stories of their lives at shivah, the week of mourning, and on each yahrzeit, the anniversary of a death.

games.q: you're naming a Torah portion. its first story is Sarah's death and burial. what do you call it?
games.why: it's Chayei Sarah, the life of Sarah, from its first words. the name points past the death to the life.

practice: Bring to mind someone you've lost, a grandparent, a friend, a teacher, even a pet, and skip past the ending for a moment. Find one ordinary scene from their life: a kitchen, a car ride, something they always said.
Stay in that scene, and let them be alive in it for a while.

wordCard.voice: Chayei Sarah. The life of Sarah: a Torah portion that opens with her death, and is named for her life. Chayim, life, is the same word in the toast l'chaim.

orig.note: Hebrew: the life of Sarah. chayei comes from chayim, life, as in l'chaim.

carryVoice: Your line: the portion is called life. Her years come first, then her death. That's day one hundred eighty-one.
